prep.tldr: Good WSET preparation means three things: picking the level that matches your knowledge, studying the syllabus chapter by chapter with active recall, and rehearsing the real exam format before the day. The Wine Goat is an independent app that turns this into a daily plan, with lessons, practice questions, flashcards and mock exams for Wine Levels 1–3 and Spirits Levels 1–2.
lead: Whether you are a curious drinker, a sommelier in training or someone who sells wine and spirits every day, a WSET qualification rewards steady, well-organised study far more than last-minute cramming. The course gives you the content; how you revise it decides how calm and confident you feel in the exam room.

This page brings together everything you need to start: how the levels differ, how much time each one asks for, a study method that works at every level, the most common mistakes, and how The Wine Goat can support your preparation in English, Italian, French or Spanish.
body: How do you prepare for a WSET exam?

Prepare in three phases: learn the syllabus chapter by chapter, consolidate it with practice questions and flashcards every day, then rehearse the real exam with timed mock exams in the final weeks. Each phase needs a small, regular effort rather than long weekend sessions.

The WSET qualifications are taught by independent course providers, in a classroom or online, and every level ends with a closed-book exam organised by your provider. Your course gives you the structure and the textbook. What happens between lessons is up to you, and that is where most results are decided: people who review a little every day remember far more than people who reread their notes the night before.

A useful way to think about it is that the course teaches you the material once, while revision makes sure you can retrieve it under time pressure. Reading feels productive, but answering questions, recalling facts from memory and explaining ideas in your own words are what actually build exam-ready knowledge.
Which WSET qualification should you prepare for?

Start at Level 1 if wine or spirits are completely new to you, at Level 2 if you already know the main grapes or categories, and at Level 3 only once you have Level 2 or equivalent knowledge. The table below compares the levels you can prepare for in The Wine Goat today.
Theory: 50 multiple-choice + 4 short written answers; blind tasting of 2 wines

Two patterns stand out. First, the pass mark drops from 70% at Level 1 to 55% at Level 2 and above, because the questions become much more detailed. Second, the workload grows quickly: Level 3 asks for roughly three times the study time of Level 2 and adds written answers and a blind tasting. Our WSET Wine Exam Preparation page compares the three wine levels in depth, and the spirits courses page does the same for spirits.
New to wine or spirits and want a fast, friendly start: Level 1.
You enjoy wine or work in a shop, bar or restaurant: Level 2 is the most popular starting point, and Level 1 is not required.
You hold Level 2 and want to understand why wines taste the way they do: Level 3.
You studied wine and now want spirits: Spirits Level 2 is usually the right entry point, since production is a separate subject.
A study method that works at every level

The most reliable method combines four habits: learn in small chapters, test yourself straight away, repeat what you forget at increasing intervals, and practise the exact exam format. These habits are backed by decades of research on memory and they suit busy schedules.
1. Learn one chapter at a time

Follow the order of the syllabus and finish one topic before moving on: grape varieties, then a region, then winemaking or distillation. Short lessons of ten to fifteen minutes are easier to fit into a day and easier to remember than a two-hour reading session.

After each lesson, answer a set of questions on the same chapter. Retrieving information from memory, even when you get it wrong, strengthens it more than rereading. Always read the explanation, and especially why the other options are wrong: that is where you learn to spot traps.

Flashcards with spaced repetition bring back the cards you miss sooner and the ones you know later. Ten minutes a day is enough to keep grape varieties, label terms, minimum ageing periods and service temperatures fresh until the exam.

In the last weeks, sit full mock exams with the real number of questions and the real time limit. Mock exams show you where you lose marks, train your pacing and remove the surprise factor on the day.
Keep a short list of your own recurring mistakes and reread it before every mock exam. Most errors repeat: the same two regions confused, the same label term misread.
How much study time do you really need?

Use the guideline hours as a minimum: about 6 hours for Level 1, around 26–28 hours for Level 2 and about 84 hours for Level 3, including class time. Spread them over the weeks before the exam rather than concentrating them.

A practical rule is to work backwards from your exam date. For Level 2, four to six weeks of 30–40 minutes a day covers the syllabus with time left for revision and mock exams. For Level 3, plan two to three months, with daily theory sessions, one written answer every day or two and regular tasting practice. If your exam is close, focus on the chapters with the most questions and on your weakest topics instead of trying to cover everything again.
From enrolment until about 3 weeks before the exam
One chapter at a time, questions after each lesson, daily flashcards
Mixed question sets across chapters, review of mistakes, weak topics first
Full timed mock exams, short daily reviews, no new material in the final days

What to do in the final week

In the last seven days, stop learning new material and focus on consolidation: one timed mock exam early in the week, short reviews of your mistakes, and daily flashcards. Sleep and a clear head are worth more than one extra chapter.
Early in the week: sit a full mock exam and list every topic that cost you marks.
Middle of the week: revise only those topics, with short question sets on each one.
Two days before: a light second mock exam or a mixed set, then stop.
The day before: flashcards only, check the exam time, place and what you need to bring.
On the day: read every question to the end, answer everything (there is no penalty for a wrong answer at Levels 1 and 2) and keep an eye on the clock.
Most candidates who struggle do not lack knowledge; they lack retrieval practice and exam rehearsal. Watch out for these habits.
Rereading the textbook instead of testing yourself.
Leaving smaller topics (fortified wines, liqueurs, labelling terms, food pairing) to the end.
Learning grapes and regions separately instead of as pairs.
Never practising under time pressure before the real exam.
At Level 3, writing lists of keywords instead of explaining cause and effect.
Studying for hours on one day and nothing for the rest of the week.

The Wine Goat's interface is available in 14 languages, and the full lessons and questions are in English, Italian, French and Spanish (with separate versions for Spain and Argentina), with more languages being added. You can study in the language you think in and switch to the language of your exam to learn the exact terminology, which is especially helpful for label terms and tasting vocabulary.

faq: How long should I study for a WSET exam?

As a guideline, Level 1 needs about 6 hours, Level 2 around 26 to 28 hours and Level 3 about 84 hours, including class time. In practice, most people do best with short daily sessions over several weeks: four to six weeks for Level 2 and two to three months for Level 3, ending with timed mock exams in the final fortnight.
Can I skip Level 1 and start with Level 2?

Yes. Level 1 is not a requirement for Level 2, and many people start directly at Level 2, especially if they already drink wine with some curiosity or work in hospitality. Level 3, on the other hand, is designed for people who already have Level 2 or equivalent knowledge, because it builds on the same grapes, regions and terms.
What is the best way to revise for a WSET multiple-choice exam?

Answer questions every day rather than rereading notes, and always read the explanations, including why the wrong options are wrong. Use flashcards with spaced repetition for facts such as label terms and ageing rules, review your own mistakes regularly, and sit at least two or three full timed mock exams before the real one.
Is The Wine Goat run by WSET?

No. The Wine Goat is an independent preparation app and is not affiliated with or endorsed by the Wine & Spirit Education Trust. Our lessons and questions are written by our own team to follow the published syllabuses. You still enrol with a WSET course provider, who teaches the course and organises your exam.
Which levels can I prepare for in The Wine Goat?

You can prepare for Wine Levels 1, 2 and 3 and Spirits Levels 1 and 2. Wine Level 1 and Spirits Level 1 are free. Spirits Level 3 and the Diploma are in preparation. Every available level includes lessons, practice questions with explanations, flashcards, mock exams, a review of your mistakes and a personal study plan.
Do I need to taste wine to prepare?

At Levels 1 and 2 there is no tasting exam, but tasting still helps you remember styles, grapes and regions. At Wine Level 3 tasting is assessed with two wines served blind, so regular practice with the systematic approach is essential. The app's tasting diary and, at Level 3, the blind-tasting trainer help you practise consistently.

lead: The three WSET wine levels share the same goal, understanding what is in the glass, but they ask very different things of you. Level 1 checks that you know the main styles and grapes, Level 2 that you can connect grapes, regions and labels, and Level 3 that you can explain why a wine tastes the way it does.
This page compares the three levels side by side, helps you pick the right one and explains how to prepare for each exam, with the tools The Wine Goat offers at every level.
body: How do the three WSET wine levels compare?

Each level adds depth and a new type of assessment: Level 1 and Level 2 use multiple-choice questions only, while Level 3 adds short written answers and a blind tasting. The study time grows from about 6 hours to about 84 hours.
50 multiple-choice + 4 short written answers, about 2 hours

Notice how the pass mark falls as the questions become harder. A 70% target at Level 1 sounds demanding, but the questions are simple; a 55% pass at Level 3 sounds generous, but you must reach it separately in the theory and in the tasting, and a strong result in one cannot compensate for the other.
WSET Wine Level 1: the first step
Level 1 is a short, beginner-friendly course on the main styles of wine, the principal grapes, storage and service, and food pairing. A few hours of focused practice are usually enough to feel ready.

The syllabus covers still, sparkling and fortified wines; how grape variety and climate shape style; the eight principal grapes (Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Syrah); service temperatures and glasses; and how sweetness, acidity, salt and umami in food change the taste of a wine. With 90 seconds per question, time is rarely the issue: careless mistakes are, because 70% leaves room for only nine wrong answers.

Learn the food and wine interactions as a small table with arrows: sweet and umami food make wine taste more bitter and acidic; salt and acidity in food make it taste softer. Directions, not definitions, are what the questions test.
WSET Wine Level 2: grapes, regions and labels

Level 2 is the most popular wine qualification: it links the principal grapes and about 22 regionally important ones to more than 70 regions, and teaches how environment, winemaking and labels explain the wines you see on shelves.

The exam is 50 multiple-choice questions in one hour, with 55% to pass, 70% for merit and 85% for distinction. The questions reward connections: a region with its grape, a climate with its style, a label term with its meaning. Typical topics include oak and malolactic conversion, the traditional and tank methods for sparkling wine, Port and Sherry, and quality categories such as Crianza, Riserva, Kabinett or AOC/DOP.
Build a grid for the eight principal grapes: climate, key regions, typical aromas, cool versus warm styles.
Learn regions as pairs with their grapes, then add the regionally important varieties country by country.
Turn labelling terms into flashcards and review them daily.
From three weeks before the exam, sit a full 50-question mock every week and aim for 70% to give yourself a margin.
WSET Wine Level 3: explain, write and taste
Level 3 asks you to explain causes and effects across the whole world of wine and to assess two wines blind. It is a significant step up and rewards regular study over two to three months.

The theory unit combines 50 multiple-choice questions with 4 short written answers, each split into parts where every mark rewards a correct, explained idea. The tasting unit asks for a full description of two wines with the systematic approach to tasting, including conclusions on quality and readiness for drinking; you are not asked to name the wine. You need at least 55% in each unit, and the units are marked separately.
Study the vineyard and winemaking chapters thoroughly first: almost every regional question relies on them.
For each region, learn the chain climate → grape → winemaking → style → label.
Write one short answer every day or two and mark it against marking points: one idea per sentence, always with the "why".
Taste with the full systematic approach on every wine you drink, using only the exam vocabulary.
Sit timed theory mocks and practise two-wine blind flights in the final weeks.
Which wine level should you choose?

Start at Level 1 if wine is completely new, at Level 2 if you already know some grapes or work with wine, and at Level 3 after Level 2 or equivalent knowledge. Skipping Level 1 is common; skipping Level 2 is rarely a good idea.
You want a friendly introduction in a short time: Level 1.
You serve or sell wine, or simply want solid foundations: Level 2, with or without Level 1 first.
You hold Level 2 and want to understand the reasons behind styles and quality: Level 3.
You work in the trade and want the widely recognised professional standard: Level 3, and later the Diploma.

If you are unsure, try a few practice questions from each level. If Level 2 questions feel comfortable, you are probably ready to aim higher; if Level 1 questions already feel hard, start there and move on while the basics are fresh.

The next step is the Level 4 Diploma in Wines, a multi-unit professional qualification that requires Level 3 and takes many months of study. It is not part of this comparison, but it is worth knowing where the path leads.

The Diploma is organised in six units, D1 to D6, combining theory and tasting exams with a research assignment. Many people take Level 3 first simply to deepen their understanding and stop there; others use it as the foundation for a career in buying, education or wine writing. If the Diploma is your long-term goal, treat Level 3 as training in method: precise vocabulary, structured written answers and consistent tasting notes will all carry over. Support for the Diploma in The Wine Goat is in preparation.
How The Wine Goat covers each wine level

Every wine level in the app comes with lessons by chapter, practice questions with explanations, flashcards with spaced repetition, mock exams in the real format, a review of your mistakes, games and a personal study plan. Level 3 adds tools for the written and tasting units.
101 open questions with model answers and marking points
Blind-tasting trainer with the systematic approach, plus tasting diary
Maps, films, podcasts, flashcards, games, study plan

The study plan starts from your exam date and target grade and sets a daily goal, so you always know what to do next. The label and glass scanner lets you save the wines you taste in "My wines", which turns everyday bottles into revision.
Common mistakes across the wine levels
The same few mistakes cost marks at every level. Most are about method rather than knowledge.
Confusing a grape with a place: Chablis is a region, Chardonnay is the grape.
Mixing up regions in the same country, such as Bordeaux Left and Right Bank or Northern and Southern Rhône.
Forgetting that the same grape tastes different in a cool and a warm climate.
Confusing sparkling methods: second fermentation in the bottle versus in a tank.
Leaving fortified wines, labelling terms and food pairing until the last week.
At Level 3, listing facts instead of explaining them, and using synonyms instead of the tasting terms the exam expects.
Whatever your level, review your mistakes before you add new material. A mistake you understand today is a question you will get right in the exam.
Translate the guideline hours into a weekly rhythm you can keep: short daily sessions beat occasional long ones at every level.
2 timed mocks in the last days
One a week in the last 3 weeks
45–60 minutes, plus a written answer every day or two and regular tasting
Theory mocks and blind flights in the last 4 weeks

Start free with Level 1, or choose Level 2 or 3, set your exam date and get a daily plan of lessons, questions, flashcards and mock exams.
faq: What is the difference between WSET Wine Level 2 and Level 3?

Level 2 tests knowledge with 50 multiple-choice questions: which grape grows where, what a label term means, how a method works. Level 3 asks you to explain why, with 50 multiple-choice questions plus 4 short written answers, and adds a blind tasting of two wines. Level 3 also requires roughly three times the study time of Level 2.
Is WSET Wine Level 1 necessary before Level 2?

No. Level 2 has no entry requirement and is written for people with little prior knowledge, so many candidates start there directly. Level 1 is still useful if wine is completely new to you or if you want a quick, confidence-building first qualification before committing to a longer course.
How hard is the WSET Wine Level 3 exam?

It is a real step up. You must pass the theory and the tasting separately, each with at least 55%, and the written answers reward explained ideas rather than lists of facts. Candidates who study regularly over two to three months, write practice answers and taste with the systematic approach are well placed to do well.
How many questions are in the WSET wine exams?

Level 1 has 30 multiple-choice questions in 45 minutes and Level 2 has 50 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes. The Level 3 theory unit has 50 multiple-choice questions and 4 short written answers, and the tasting unit asks you to describe two wines served blind.
Can I prepare for all three wine levels in The Wine Goat?

Yes. Wine Levels 1, 2 and 3 are all available. Level 1 is free, Level 2 has about 1,070 practice questions and Level 3 has more than 2,000, plus 101 open questions with model answers and marking points, a blind-tasting trainer, maps, films and podcasts. Each level includes mock exams in the real format.

mock.title: WSET Mock Exams and Practice Tests
mock.desc: How to use WSET mock exams: the format of each level, how to sit a mock in real conditions, how to review your score and the mistakes that cost you marks.

mock.tldr: A WSET mock exam is a full practice paper sat with the real number of questions and the real time limit. Sitting two or three mocks in the final weeks, then reviewing every mistake, is the most effective way to find weak topics, train your pacing and walk into the exam without surprises.
lead: You can know the syllabus well and still lose marks in the exam room: a question read too fast, a topic you never revised, a clock you forgot to watch. Mock exams exist to remove those risks before they count.
This page explains why mock exams work, how to sit one properly, how to review the result, what the format of each WSET level looks like, and how The Wine Goat simulates them for wine and spirits.
body: Why do mock exams matter for WSET?
Mock exams test what you can retrieve under time pressure, not what you recognise in your notes. They reveal your weak chapters, train your pacing and make the real exam feel familiar.

Practice questions by chapter are excellent while you learn, but they give you a hint: you know the topic before you read the question. In the real exam, a question on Sherry follows one on Riesling and another on storage. A mock exam mixes the whole syllabus exactly as the paper does, so it measures the knowledge you can actually use on the day.

Mock exams also give you a realistic score. If you consistently reach 70% or more in Level 2 mocks, you have a comfortable margin over the 55% pass mark. If you hover around the pass mark, you know you need to act on your weak topics before the exam, not after.
What is the format of each WSET exam?

Levels 1 and 2 are multiple-choice papers with a fixed number of questions and minutes; Wine Level 3 combines multiple-choice questions, short written answers and a blind tasting. A good mock reproduces exactly that.
At least 55% in the theory unit
At least 55% in the tasting unit

Every question carries one mark at Levels 1 and 2 and there is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a question blank. At Level 3, the theory and tasting units are marked separately: a strong theory score cannot compensate for a weak tasting, or the other way round.
How to sit a mock exam in real conditions
Treat the mock like the real exam: one sitting, the real time limit, no notes, no phone and no pausing. The closer the conditions, the more useful the result.
Choose a quiet moment when you will not be interrupted for the whole duration.
Set the real time limit and do not stop the clock, even for one question.
Close your notes, textbook and other apps; the exam is closed book.
Answer every question, flagging the ones you are unsure about to revisit at the end.
Check the clock at the halfway point: at Level 2 you should be around question 25 after 30 minutes.
For Level 3 written answers, write in full sentences as you would on the day, not in notes.
Do your mock at the same time of day as your real exam if you can. Your concentration curve is part of what you are training.
How to review a mock exam
The review is where the progress happens: spend at least as long reviewing a mock as you spent sitting it. Classify every mistake, then fix the cause, not just the question.
Sort your mistakes into three types
Knowledge gaps: you did not know the fact. Go back to the lesson for that chapter and add the fact to your flashcards.
Confusions: you mixed up two similar things, such as two regions, two methods or two label terms. Build a small comparison of the pair.
Reading errors: you knew the answer but missed a word such as "not", "minimum" or "main". Slow down on the question stem.
Look at the chapter, not only the score

A total of 68% hides very different situations. Losing marks evenly across the syllabus means you need broad revision; losing half of them in one chapter means a targeted session will lift your score quickly. Check your results by topic and plan the next few days around the two or three weakest ones.
Read the explanations of correct answers too
Some correct answers were lucky guesses. If you hesitated, read the explanation anyway and learn why the other options are wrong: that is how you will recognise the same trap next time.
When should you sit mock exams?

Sit your first full mock about three weeks before the exam, then one per week, and a final light one two or three days before. Earlier than that, chapter questions are more useful because you have not covered the whole syllabus yet.
First full mock: a baseline score and a list of weak chapters
Second mock after targeted revision; compare scores chapter by chapter
Third mock; aim for a safety margin above the pass mark
A light mixed set or a final mock, then only flashcards and your mistakes list

At Level 1 the timeline is shorter: two timed mocks in the last few days are usually enough. At Wine Level 3, add timed written answers every week and practise two-wine blind flights, describing each wine fully with the systematic approach.
Mock practice for Level 3 written answers and tasting
At Wine Level 3, a multiple-choice mock is only half of the rehearsal. Practise the written answers and the tasting under time pressure too, because they are where most marks are won or lost.

Each short written answer is divided into parts, and the marks for each part tell you how many separate ideas the examiner expects. Practise reading the question twice, underlining the command words (describe, explain, compare) and planning your points before writing. Then mark yourself honestly against marking points: one mark for each correct, explained idea, nothing for a keyword without its reason.
The cool climate slows ripening, so the grapes keep high acidity, giving a fresh, light-bodied wine.
Maturation in new oak barrels adds vanilla and toast flavours and allows slow oxygen contact, which softens the tannins.

For the tasting unit, pour two wines without looking at the labels and write a complete note for each in a set time: appearance, nose, palate and conclusions on quality and readiness for drinking. Check every structural element (sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, flavour intensity, finish) and justify your quality assessment with balance, length, intensity and complexity.
Mock exams only help if they are honest. These habits make them less useful.
Sitting the same mock again and again until you remember the answers rather than the reasons.
Pausing the clock or checking notes, which gives you a score you cannot trust.
Looking only at the final percentage and skipping the review.
Taking the first mock too late to act on the results.
At Level 3, skipping the written section because it takes longer to mark.
Panicking after one low score: a mock is a diagnosis, not a verdict.
The Wine Goat's mock exams mirror the real format and timing of each available level, with a fresh mix of questions drawn from the whole syllabus and a detailed review at the end.
Wine and Spirits Level 1: 30 questions in 45 minutes, with the 70% pass mark.
Wine and Spirits Level 2: 50 questions in 60 minutes, with pass, merit and distinction thresholds.
Wine Level 3 theory: 50 multiple-choice questions plus 4 short written answers, with model answers and marking points to check your writing.
Results by chapter, so you see immediately which topics need work.
Every mistake goes into your personal review and comes back in later sessions until you get it right.
Explanations for each question, including why the other options are wrong.

Your study plan schedules mock exams automatically as the exam date approaches, alongside daily lessons, questions and flashcards. For the Level 3 tasting unit, the blind-tasting trainer helps you practise full descriptions with the systematic approach. faq: How many mock exams should I do before a WSET exam?

Two or three full mocks in the final three weeks are enough for most candidates at Level 2, provided you review each one carefully. At Level 1, two timed mocks in the last days usually suffice. At Level 3, combine weekly theory mocks with regular timed written answers and blind tastings of two wines.
What score in a mock exam means I am ready?

Aim for a safety margin above the pass mark. At Level 2, consistently scoring 70% or more in mocks gives you room for nerves on the day; at Level 1, aim for 80% or more because the pass mark is already 70%. At Level 3, check that both the multiple-choice and the written sections are comfortably above 55%.
Are WSET mock exams the same as the real exam questions?

No. Mock exams in The Wine Goat are written by our own team to reproduce the format, timing and difficulty of the real exam, but they are not past papers. Their value lies in practising the syllabus under realistic conditions and finding your weak topics, not in memorising specific questions.
How long is the WSET Level 2 exam?

The WSET Level 2 exam, for both wine and spirits, is 50 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes, which gives you 72 seconds per question. You need 55% to pass, 70% for merit and 85% for distinction. There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question.
Should I repeat the same mock exam?

Repeating a mock straight away mostly tests your memory of the answers. It is better to sit a fresh mix of questions each time and to revisit your mistakes separately. In The Wine Goat, each mock draws a new set from the whole syllabus, and your mistakes come back in your personal review.
Can I do a mock exam for the Level 3 written answers?

Yes. The Wine Level 3 mock in The Wine Goat includes 4 short written answers alongside the 50 multiple-choice questions. After writing your answers, you compare them with model answers and marking points, which shows whether you explained each idea clearly enough to earn the mark.

lead: The WSET exams at Levels 1 and 2 are entirely multiple-choice, and Wine Level 3 starts with 50 multiple-choice questions before the written answers. Being good at this format is a skill in itself: it rewards precise knowledge, careful reading and a calm pace.

This page explains how to use practice questions well, shares a simple technique for answering multiple-choice questions, and gives you 12 sample questions with explanations so you can test yourself right now.
body: Answering a question forces your memory to retrieve information, and every successful retrieval makes the next one easier. That is why testing yourself beats rereading, even when you get answers wrong.

Reading a chapter twice feels like progress because the text looks familiar. But familiarity is not recall: in the exam you have to produce the answer from memory, among three plausible alternatives. Practice questions train exactly that. They also show you, quickly and honestly, which topics you really know and which ones you only recognise.

Good questions come with explanations. A short note on why the right answer is right consolidates the fact; a deeper look at why each other option is wrong teaches you the distinctions the exam is built on, such as two regions that grow the same grape or two methods that sound alike.
How to use practice questions in your revision
Use questions at three moments: straight after each lesson, in mixed sets across chapters, and in full mock exams near the end. Short daily sets are more effective than occasional long ones.
Questions on that chapter only, read every explanation
Mixed questions from chapters you have already studied, plus your past mistakes

Write down or save every question you get wrong and revisit it a few days later.

Read the whole question, predict the answer before looking at the options, eliminate the clearly wrong ones and only then choose. Never leave a question blank: there is no penalty for a wrong answer at Levels 1 and 2.

Many questions hinge on one word: "main", "typically", "minimum", "not", "most likely". Underline it mentally before you read the options. A question asking which grape is not permitted is the opposite of one asking which grape is typical, and in a hurry they look the same.
Try to answer before reading the four options. If your prediction is among them, it is very probably correct. If not, reread the question: you may have misread it.

Wrong options are rarely absurd. They are often a real grape from the wrong region, a real technique with the wrong effect, or a correct fact that does not answer the question. Removing two options usually leaves a 50-50 choice you can reason through.
You have 90 seconds per question at Level 1 and 72 seconds at Level 2. Answer the easy ones quickly, flag the difficult ones and come back to them at the end with a fresh eye.
Change an answer only if you find a concrete reason, such as a word you misread. Second-guessing without new information more often turns a right answer into a wrong one.
Level 1 questions test the main grapes, styles, service and food pairing. They are short and direct; precision is what matters.
Which of these grape varieties is used to make white wine?
Riesling is a white grape variety, one of the eight principal grapes. Merlot, Syrah and Pinot Noir are all black grapes used for red (and sometimes rosé) wines.
How does salt in food usually affect the taste of a wine?
It makes the wine taste less bitter and less acidic
It makes the wine taste more acidic
It makes the wine taste more bitter
It has no effect on the wine
Salt, like acidity in food, makes a wine taste softer: less bitter and less acidic. Sweetness and umami in food have the opposite effect, making wine taste more bitter and acidic.
Which of these wines should be served well chilled?
Sparkling and sweet wines are served well chilled. Full- and medium-bodied reds are served at room temperature, while light-bodied reds can be lightly chilled.
Level 2 questions connect grapes, regions, winemaking and labels. Expect plausible distractors from the same country or technique family.
Sancerre, in the Loire Valley, is mainly made from which grape variety?

Sancerre is a classic Loire Valley wine made from Sauvignon Blanc. Chenin Blanc is also a Loire grape, which makes it a typical distractor, but it is associated with other Loire appellations such as Vouvray.
What is the main effect of malolactic conversion on a wine?
It softens the acidity and can add buttery flavours
It adds tannin to the wine
It leaves residual sugar in the wine

Malolactic conversion turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, lowering the perceived acidity and often adding buttery notes. It does not change the alcohol level, add tannin or create sweetness.
Which method is typically used to make Prosecco?

Prosecco is typically made by the tank method, with the second fermentation in a sealed tank, which preserves fresh, fruity aromas. The traditional method, with the second fermentation in the bottle, is used for Champagne.
Level 3 multiple-choice questions focus on causes and effects. Knowing the name is not enough: you must know why it matters.
What is the main effect of a large diurnal range on ripening grapes?
Cool nights help the grapes retain acidity and aromas
It increases the risk of hail
It reduces sugar accumulation during the day

A large difference between day and night temperatures lets grapes ripen in warm days while cool nights slow the loss of acidity and help preserve aromatic compounds. It is not linked to hail, and it does not stop sugar or tannin ripening.
What does extended lees contact typically add to a still white wine?
Body, texture and yeasty or bready notes
Ageing on the lees adds body and a creamy texture, and can bring yeasty, bready flavours. Lees contact does not add tannin or colour, does not raise acidity and does not make a wine sweet.
How is the sweetness of Port achieved?
By drying the grapes before fermentation
By adding grape spirit during fermentation, which stops it
By blending in unfermented grape juice
Port is fortified during fermentation: the grape spirit raises the alcohol level and stops the yeast, leaving natural grape sugar in the wine. This is why Port is both sweet and high in alcohol.
Spirits questions often test raw materials, legal rules and label terms. Numbers such as minimum percentages and ageing periods are easy marks once memorised.
What is a legal requirement for Bourbon?
It must be made in Kentucky
It must be made from 100% malted barley
It can use any grain, with no minimum
It must be made from a mash of at least 51% corn

Bourbon must be made from at least 51% corn and aged in new charred oak barrels. It can be made anywhere in the United States, not only in Kentucky; 100% malted barley is the rule for single malt whisky.
A Tequila labelled "joven" or "oro" is usually:
Aged for at least one year in oak
Unaged spirit, often with colour added
Made from a blend of Tequila and Mezcal
Aged in new charred oak barrels
Joven or oro (gold) Tequila is usually unaged, with colour added; the golden hue does not mean oak ageing. Reposado and añejo are the terms for Tequilas that have spent time in oak.
What is the minimum ageing for a Cognac labelled VSOP?
VSOP Cognac must be aged for at least four years in oak. VS requires at least two years and XO at least ten, so these terms make classic distractors for each other.
How to learn from a wrong answer
A wrong answer is the most useful thing a practice session can give you, provided you deal with it in three steps: understand it, connect it, and see it again later.
Understand: read the explanation and say in one sentence why the correct answer is right.
Connect: link the fact to something you already know, such as the climate of the region or the effect of the technique, so it is not an isolated detail.
Compare: if you confused two similar things, write the difference between them side by side.
Repeat: answer the same question again a few days later, and once more the week before the exam.

Are these the real WSET exam questions?

No. Our questions are written by our own team to follow the published syllabuses and to reproduce the style and difficulty of the exam. They are not past papers. Their purpose is to help you practise retrieving the knowledge the exam tests, not to memorise specific questions.
How many practice questions should I do per day?

Quality matters more than quantity. Around 10 to 15 questions after each lesson, plus a mixed set of 15 to 25 questions on topics you have already studied, is a good daily rhythm. What makes the difference is reading every explanation and revisiting your mistakes a few days later.
Is there negative marking in WSET multiple-choice exams?

At Levels 1 and 2, each correct answer earns one mark and a wrong answer simply earns nothing, so there is no reason to leave any question blank. If you are unsure, eliminate the options you know are wrong and make your best choice from what remains.
Do practice questions help with the Level 3 written answers?
